docs.title: alert-triage-economics
docs.text:
"We reduced false positives by 60 percent" is one of the most common sentences in SOC reporting and one of the least often costed. The sentence has a second half that nobody collects: and it cost us this many real detections.

This tool computes that second half. Feed it a labelled alert stream and it reports, per rule, what every candidate threshold would have removed and what it would have cost.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Reading the frontier explains the chart and what each shape means.
  • The statistics covers separation, intervals, and the three verdicts, including why "we do not know" needed to be one of them.
  • The example report is regenerated on every docs deploy from the bundled synthetic corpus.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install alert-triage-economics

docs.title: The shortest useful run
docs.text:
ate generate --alerts 500000 --out alerts.parquet --seed 7
ate frontier --alerts alerts.parquet --out report.html

The first command exists so the tool can be evaluated without exporting anything real. Replace it with your own three column export, rule, signal and is_true_positive, and the numbers stop being a simulation.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• ADR-001: why every statistic ships with an interval.
  • ADR-002: capping the resampled noise pool, with the measurement.
  • ADR-003: the synthetic corpus, and the rule in it that cannot be tuned.
  • ADR-004: leading with the stable number rather than the intuitive one.
  • ADR-005: the third verdict, and the measurement behind its threshold.

docs.title: Reading the frontier
docs.text: Each line is one rule. The x axis is the share of that rule's alert volume a threshold would remove. The y axis is the share of that rule's true positives that would go with it.

docs.title: The diagonal
docs.text:
The dotted diagonal is the reference that makes the rest of the chart mean something: remove half the volume, lose half the detections. That is what tuning a rule whose signal carries no information looks like. You are not tuning, you are sampling.

Every rule should be read against it.

docs.title: Shapes and what they mean
docs.text:
A line hugging the bottom left then rising late. The signal separates well. A large share of volume can go before detections start falling. This is a rule worth tuning and the chart says where to stop.

A line on or above the diagonal. The signal is noise, or worse than noise if it is above. Any threshold deletes detections at least as fast as it deletes volume. Do not tune this rule; fix the signal or accept the volume.

Check the verdict before concluding that, though. If the rule reads unknown the line is drawn from too few detections to mean anything, and its position relative to the diagonal is noise rather than evidence.

A staircase. Few detections. Each step is one true positive dropping out, so a rule with twelve of them has twelve steps. Staircases are a visual warning that the curve is built from very little. A staircase drawn dash dotted in amber is one the tool has refused to judge at all, and its label carries the detection count.

A line that bows well below the diagonal but starts rising immediately. The signal separates, but the lowest scoring detection sits low. Free volume will be small even though the rule is genuinely tunable. This is the case where the blanket cut figures are more useful than the free volume one.

docs.title: What the table adds
docs.text:
The chart shows shape. The table shows whether the shape is trustworthy.

Separation is the probability a random true positive outscores a random noise alert. 0.5 is no information, 1.0 is perfect. It is the single number summary of how far the line bows from the diagonal.

The interval on separation is what decides tunability, where there are enough detections to decide at all. A rule can show a point estimate of 0.54, which looks faintly promising, on an interval of 0.38 to 0.69, which includes chance.

The verdict column reads yes, no or unknown. unknown means fewer detections than the configured minimum, and it is a different finding from no: the window is too short, rather than the signal being useless. The bundled corpus contains exactly that rule, on purpose, and ADR-005 explains why an interval alone cannot catch it.

Removable free is the volume removable with zero detections lost. Read it with the caveat in ADR-004: it depends on the length of the window, because it is determined by the single lowest scoring detection in it. A longer export produces a smaller number for the same rule.

Lost at 50 percent is stable across window lengths and is the figure to quote when somebody proposes a volume target.

docs.title: The question the chart cannot answer
docs.text: What an attacker would have done differently had the threshold been in place. This is a replay: it says what would have happened to these alerts. Nothing about a historical replay licenses a claim about future adversary behaviour, and a tuning that looks free here can still change what gets attempted.

docs.title: The statistics
docs.text: Three numbers per rule, each with an interval. This page says what they are, how they are computed, and where each one breaks.

docs.title: Separation
docs.text:
The probability that a randomly chosen true positive scores higher on the tuning signal than a randomly chosen noise alert.

This is the Mann Whitney U statistic normalised by the product of the class sizes, which is the same quantity as the area under an ROC curve. It is computed from ranks rather than by sampling pairs, so it is exact rather than estimated:

U = rank_sum(positives) - n_pos * (n_pos + 1) / 2
separation = U / (n_pos * n_neg)

0.5 means the signal carries no information about whether an alert is real. 1.0 means it separates perfectly. Below 0.5 means the signal is inverted, which is a real finding and usually a configuration error.

Where it breaks. It says nothing about where on the curve the separation lives. Two rules can share a separation of 0.75 while one allows a generous free cut and the other does not. Read it with the chart, never instead of it.

docs.title: Removable free volume
docs.text:
The largest share of a rule's volume that can be removed while losing zero true positives. Equivalently: everything scoring below the lowest scoring detection.

Where it breaks. It is an order statistic of the minimum, so it depends on how long the window is. More detections means a lower worst one means a smaller figure. On a fixed stream it fell from 17.3 to 2.7 percent as the corpus grew from 50,000 to 2,000,000 alerts. ADR-004 has the measurement and is the reason this is not the headline number.

It is still the right answer to "what can we remove from this export today".

docs.title: Blanket cut cost
docs.text:
The share of true positives lost if a flat percentage of every rule's volume is removed, including the rules that cannot be tuned.

This is the number that answers a volume reduction target. It is stable across window lengths, which is why the report leads with it.

Where it breaks. It assumes the cut is applied uniformly, which is a deliberately pessimistic model of how tuning is actually done. A team tuning rule by rule, guided by the frontier, will do better than this figure. It is the cost of the blunt version of the instruction, and the blunt version is what a volume target usually becomes.

docs.title: The intervals
docs.text:
Every published statistic carries a bootstrap percentile interval, by default 2000 stratified replicates at 95 percent.

Stratified means true positives and noise alerts are resampled within their own classes, so every replicate holds the same number of detections as the original. This is a requirement rather than a refinement: an unstratified bootstrap on a rule with twelve detections produces replicates holding one or two, where the statistics are defined but meaningless, and the resulting interval describes the procedure rather than the rule.

The noise pool is capped at 20,000 draws per replicate. Both statistics have sampling variance dominated by the detection count, so the cap discards precision the result could never have used. ADR-002 has the table, and a test asserts the claim rather than leaving it to the document.

docs.title: The three verdicts
docs.text:
tunable, not_tunable, insufficient_evidence. Three states, because two cannot say the thing that most often needs saying.

tunable means the lower bound of the separation interval clears 0.5, and the rule has at least the minimum number of detections. Not the point estimate: a rule showing 0.54 on an interval of 0.38 to 0.69 has not demonstrated anything.

not_tunable means there are enough detections to judge and the interval does not clear chance. The signal is the problem. Fix the signal or accept the volume.

insufficient_evidence means there are fewer detections than the minimum, which defaults to 20. The answer is that we do not know, whatever the interval reads. The window is the problem, not the signal.

docs.title: Why the third state exists
docs.text:
A bootstrap resamples the detections it has. With six of them it measures how the statistic moves under reweighting those six, which is a real quantity and not the one that matters: it has nothing to compare them against to notice they are unrepresentative. If all six score high, every replicate scores high, and the interval comes out narrow around a badly wrong estimate.

That is not hypothetical. The bundled corpus contains a rule with no signal at all by construction. On a 200,000 alert window it holds six detections, and the tool reported separation 0.804 with a 95 percent interval of 0.611 to 0.960. Narrow, confident, clear of chance, and wrong.

ADR-005 has the sweep behind the threshold: on a pure noise signal a tunable verdict came back 3 to 5 percent of the time below 20 detections, and never at or above it.

docs.title: Why not collapse unmeasured into untunable
docs.text:
It would give the same safety behaviour and the wrong instruction. An untunable rule needs a better signal, which is a redesign. An unmeasured rule needs a longer window, which is an export. Telling an engineer the first when the second is true sends them to rewrite a rule that may be perfectly good.

insufficient_evidence never reads as tunable, so the conservative direction holds either way. Suppressing alerts is irreversible in a way that not suppressing them is not.

docs.title: ADR-001: Bootstrap intervals rather than point estimates
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This tool exists to replace a sentence: "we reduced false positives by 60 percent". The problem with that sentence is not the 60 percent, it is that it is reported alone, with no statement of what it cost or how certain it is. Replacing it with a different bare number would reproduce the same error with better arithmetic.

The arithmetic matters here more than it does in most places. A SOC's alert stream is severely imbalanced: the bundled corpus runs at roughly one true positive per 300 alerts, which is deliberately in the range public SOC reporting describes. One rule in that corpus produces 45,000 alerts and 12 true positives.

Every statistic this tool computes about that rule is a statistic about twelve observations.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Point estimates only. Report separation as 0.537 and removable volume as 12.7 percent. Rejected: both figures are computed from twelve true positives and a reader has no way to see that. The 12.7 percent figure in particular is dangerous, because it looks like a tuning opportunity on a rule that has no usable signal at all.
  2. A normal approximation interval. Cheap, and wrong at these counts: the sampling distribution of a rank statistic on twelve positives is not symmetric and the approximation produces intervals that extend past the statistic's own range.
  3. Analytic intervals for the rank statistic. Available for the separation statistic, which is the Mann Whitney U, but not for the removable volume figure, which is an order statistic of the positive class with no convenient closed form. Two different interval methods in one table would invite the reader to compare numbers that are not comparable.
  4. Stratified bootstrap percentile intervals for both. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Report a bootstrap percentile interval alongside every published statistic, and decide tunability from the interval rather than the point estimate. A rule is reported tunable only when the lower bound of its separation interval clears 0.5, which is the value a signal carrying no information would produce.

Resampling is stratified: true positives and noise alerts are resampled within their own classes, so every replicate holds the same number of true positives as the original.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The stratification is not a refinement, it is a requirement. An unstratified bootstrap on a rule with twelve true positives draws replicates containing zero of them with probability around 0.0000006 per replicate, which sounds negligible until you consider that replicates with one or two positives are common, and in those the separation statistic is defined but meaningless. The interval would then describe the resampling procedure rather than the rule.

Deciding tunability from the lower bound makes the tool conservative in the direction that matters. The bundled corpus contains a rule whose point estimate for removable volume is 12.7 percent, which reads as a real opportunity, while its separation interval runs from 0.38 to 0.69 and straddles chance. Acting on the point estimate would mean suppressing 12.7 percent of a rule's volume on the strength of where twelve detections happened to land.

The cost is runtime: every statistic is computed 2000 times instead of once. ADR-002 covers what was done about that.

The confidence level and resample count are configuration rather than constants, because a reader who wants a 99 percent interval should get one without editing the source.

docs.title: ADR-002: Cap the noise pool per bootstrap replicate
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-001 committed the tool to 2000 bootstrap replicates per rule. The first implementation rebuilt the entire frontier curve inside each replicate in order to read two numbers off it, and resampled the full noise class every time.

On the bundled corpus, eight rules at 2000 replicates took over 400 seconds. A 400 second analysis is one that gets run once and then not again, which defeats the purpose of shipping it as a CI gate.

Two separate costs were at work. Rebuilding the curve sorts and accumulates over the whole rule, when both statistics have closed forms that need one sort. Resampling 100,000 noise alerts per replicate dominates that sort, when the sampling variance of both statistics is driven by the positive count.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Fewer replicates. Rejected. The interval is the product here, and 200 replicates gives a visibly lumpy percentile estimate at these counts.
  2. Parallelism. Rejected for v1: it multiplies the hardware rather than removing the work, and the result stops being reproducible from a seed alone unless the work is partitioned carefully.
  3. Analytic interval for separation, bootstrap only for removable volume. Rejected under ADR-001's reasoning: two interval methods in one table are not comparable.
  4. Compute both statistics directly and cap the resampled noise pool. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Compute the two replicate statistics in closed form rather than from the curve, and draw at most bootstrap_noise_cap noise alerts per replicate, defaulting to 20,000. The positive class is always resampled in full.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
On a rule with 100,000 alerts and 238 true positives, 300 replicates each:

Noise pool Time Separation interval Width Full, 99,762 3.93 s [0.8117, 0.8608] 0.0492 50,000 1.76 s [0.8065, 0.8609] 0.0544 20,000 0.67 s [0.8114, 0.8591] 0.0477 10,000 0.32 s [0.8093, 0.8581] 0.0488

The same comparison on a rule with 12 true positives produced interval widths of 0.2082 uncapped and 0.2211 at 20,000, against a point estimate uncertainty that spans a third of the statistic's range.

The variation between cap levels is smaller than the variation between seeds at the same cap, which is the test: the cap is not changing the answer, it is changing how long the answer takes. A full run of eight rules at 2000 replicates went from over 400 seconds to 34.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The justification is statistical rather than a shortcut, and it is worth stating precisely: both statistics are functions of where the positive class sits within the combined distribution. The noise class defines that distribution, and 20,000 draws estimate it to a precision far beyond what 12 to 465 positives can resolve. Capping it discards precision the result could never have used.

This holds because the cap is large relative to the positive count. It would not hold for a rule with tens of thousands of true positives, which is not a rule anybody needs this tool for, and the cap is configuration rather than a constant so that case can be handled by raising it.

A test asserts the claim directly rather than trusting this document: it computes a frontier capped and uncapped on the same fixture and requires the interval bounds to agree within 0.02.

The closed form statistics are a separate change bundled into the same decision. A test asserts they produce exactly what the curve based path produces, because the curve is the definition and the fast path is only an optimisation.

docs.title: ADR-003: Ship a synthetic corpus, and put a rule in it that cannot be tuned
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This tool needs labelled alerts: alerts where somebody has recorded whether each one was a real detection. That data is the most sensitive thing a SOC holds. It contains usernames, hostnames, the shape of an organisation's detections, and the record of which attacks got through. No portfolio repository can ship it.

The options are therefore a public dataset, a corpus derived from one, or a generated corpus.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. A public intrusion detection dataset such as the CIC or UNSW families. Rejected for this specific purpose. Those datasets label network flows as attack or benign, which is a different question from whether a SOC alert was worth an analyst's time, and their class balance is nothing like a real alert queue because they were built to train classifiers rather than to describe a triage workload.
  2. A corpus derived from public honeypot or malware feeds. Rejected: the labels describe the sample, not an analyst's disposition of an alert, so the derivation would be inventing the labels while appearing not to.
  3. A generated corpus with the generator in the repository. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Generate the corpus from a declared specification that ships in the repository, seeded for reproducibility, and label every figure derived from it as a simulation at the point it is published, including in badges.

Two properties of the specification are load bearing and neither is incidental.

The imbalance is severe and stated. Roughly one true positive per 300 alerts overall, with per rule rates between 0.03 and 1.1 percent. A corpus with a comfortable 10 percent true positive rate would make every rule look tunable and the whole exercise would prove nothing. A test asserts the rate stays below one percent, so the corpus cannot drift comfortable.

One rule has no frontier at all. ids_signature_generic has a signal that carries no information about whether an alert is real. No threshold on it removes noise faster than it removes detections. A test asserts the bundled specification still contains such a rule.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The second property is the one worth defending in an interview. A corpus where every rule can be tuned is a corpus built to flatter the tool, and a tool evaluated only against flattering data will confidently recommend tuning rules that should not be tuned. The untunable rule is in the corpus specifically so that the tool has an opportunity to get it wrong, and the test that asserts the rule is reported untunable is the most valuable test in the repository.

It also happens to produce the most useful output the tool generates. That rule reports a removable volume of 12.7 percent, which looks like an opportunity, on the strength of twelve detections. Only the interval reveals it. That single contrast is the argument for ADR-001 made concrete, and it would not exist if the corpus had been built to be tuned successfully.

The honest limitation: the signal model is two normal distributions, one shifted. That is a textbook model, not a claim about how real alert signals are distributed, which are often bounded, skewed or piled up on round numbers.

It matters less than it first appears, and that is worth being precise about rather than waving away. Both published statistics are rank based: separation is the normalised Mann Whitney U, and removable volume is a position in the sorted order. Neither changes under any strictly increasing transform of the signal. A real signal that is log normal, or bounded to 0 and 1, or rounded to a 0 to 10 confidence score, has the same separation as the normal variate it is a transform of, and its frontier has the same shape.

So the normality of the generator is not load bearing for anything the tool publishes. tests/test_frontier.py::test_separation_is_invariant_under_a_monotone_transform asserts this across five transforms including a heavily tied discrete score, rather than leaving it as a claim in a document.

What does change under a real distribution is the relationship between a threshold and a volume, which is why the report shows thresholds on the curve in the signal's own units and never interprets them.

A real corpus would still be more faithful, and the roadmap records running against one as the next step.

docs.title: ADR-004: Lead with the blanket cut cost, not the free volume
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The tool produces two headline candidates and the obvious one is wrong.

Free volume is the share of a rule's alerts removable without losing a single detection. It is the number a SOC lead wants, it is intuitive, and it is what the first version of this README led with.

Blanket cut cost is the share of true positives lost if a flat percentage of every rule's volume is removed. It is less intuitive and it is the number that actually refutes an uncosted tuning claim.

The benchmark across three corpus sizes exposed the problem:

Corpus Free volume Cost of halving 50,000 alerts 17.3 percent 16.8 percent 500,000 alerts 6.5 percent 15.6 percent 2,000,000 alerts 2.7 percent 16.2 percent

Free volume moved by a factor of six across the same stream. The cost of halving barely moved at all.

docs.title: Why free volume is unstable
docs.text:
It is an order statistic of the minimum. Free volume is determined entirely by where the single lowest scoring true positive in the window happens to sit: every alert below it is removable, and nothing below it is. A longer window contains more detections, so it contains a lower worst one, so the figure shrinks. Isolated on a single rule with the separation and true positive rate held fixed:

Window True positives Separation Free volume 5,000 20 0.802 11.9 percent 20,000 80 0.816 7.5 percent 100,000 400 0.845 4.7 percent 400,000 1,600 0.848 2.6 percent

Separation is stable to three decimal places. Free volume falls by a factor of four and would keep falling, because the minimum of a sample has no limit other than the support of the distribution.

This is not a bug in the computation. It is the statistic answering exactly the question it was asked, and the question containing a hidden dependence on how long you watched.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Lead with free volume anyway. Rejected once the benchmark showed it moving by a factor of six on the same stream. A headline figure that depends on the export window is a figure a reader will quote in one meeting and be contradicted on in the next.
  2. Drop free volume. Rejected: it is the right answer to "what can we remove today", which is a real question, and it is correct for the window it was computed on.
  3. Report free volume at a fixed window. Rejected as a false fix. Fixing the window makes the figure comparable between runs while leaving it arbitrary, and hides the dependence rather than disclosing it.
  4. Lead with the blanket cut cost, keep free volume with its caveat. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The README, the report and the badge lead with the cost of halving volume. Free volume stays in the report, in the tiles rather than the headline, and the window dependence is stated wherever it appears.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The headline is now the number that does the work this tool was built for. "We cut alert volume in half" is the claim; "that costs 15.6 percent of your detections" is the reply, and it is a reply that holds whether the analysis ran on a week or a quarter.

Free volume keeps its interval, which already communicated some of this: on the 500,000 alert corpus the interval on one rule runs from 1.1 to 13.9 percent, which is a reader's clue that the point estimate is soft. The interval captures sampling variation at a fixed window, though, not the window dependence itself, so the caveat is written out rather than left to the interval.

A test asserts the direction: free volume must not increase as the window grows on a stream with fixed properties. If a change ever makes free volume look stable, something has been smoothed over.

The honest framing for anyone reading the output: free volume says what is removable from this export. The blanket cut cost says what tuning costs. Only the second one is a property of the detections rather than of the window.

docs.title: ADR-005: A third verdict for rules with too few detections
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-001 committed the tool to deciding tunability from the lower bound of a bootstrap interval rather than from a point estimate. That is the right call and it is not sufficient, which a CI threshold check exposed by accident.

The bundled corpus contains ids_signature_generic, a rule whose signal carries no information about whether an alert is real. It is in the corpus specifically so the tool has a chance to get it wrong. At 500,000 alerts it holds 12 detections, the tool reported it untunable, and that looked like the safety property working.

Then the same rule was analysed on a 200,000 alert corpus, where it holds 6 detections:

separation 0.804, 95 percent interval [0.611, 0.960], verdict: tunable

A confident, narrow interval, comfortably clear of chance, on a rule whose true separation is 0.5 by construction. The tool recommended tuning a rule that cannot be tuned, and the interval gave no warning at all.

docs.title: Why the interval cannot catch this
docs.text:
A bootstrap resamples the observed data. With six detections it draws those same six, over and over, in different multiplicities. It therefore measures how much the statistic moves under reweighting of the observed sample, which is a real quantity and not the one that matters here. What it cannot measure is whether those six detections are representative of the rule, because it has nothing else to compare them to. If all six happened to score high, every replicate scores high, and the interval is narrow around a badly wrong estimate.

The earlier correct verdict at 12 detections was not the safety property working. It was luck.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
A signal with no information at all, 20,000 alerts, 60 independent draws per detection count, asking how often the tool returned a tunable verdict:

Detections False tunable rate Median interval width 3 5.0 percent 0.600 5 3.3 percent 0.458 8 3.3 percent 0.397 12 3.3 percent 0.316 20 0.0 percent 0.247 30 0.0 percent 0.202 50 0.0 percent 0.160 100 0.0 percent 0.114

docs.title: Correction: the zeros above were underpowered
docs.text:
The table above says 0.0 percent at 20 detections and beyond. That is 0 out of 60 draws, which is consistent with any true rate below about 5 percent, and the first version of this document read it as evidence that the false rate went to zero. It does not.

A test written for an unrelated accessibility change hit a rule with 100 detections and no signal at all, reported tunable with an interval of 0.508 to 0.618. Re-running the sweep at 250 draws per count:

Detections Draws False tunable rate 20 250 4.8 percent 30 250 3.6 percent 50 250 3.2 percent 100 250 2.0 percent

The rate does not go to zero above the threshold. It settles at roughly the 5 percent a 95 percent interval promises, which is not a defect: a confidence interval that never contained a wrong answer would not be a confidence interval. Raising the detection minimum does not remove that and nothing can, short of raising the confidence level and accepting wider intervals everywhere.

docs.title: What the threshold actually buys
docs.text:
The failure below 20 detections is a different thing from the nominal error rate above it, and conflating the two is what the first version of this document did.

Above the threshold, a false tunable verdict comes with a wide interval that barely clears 0.5. The 100 detection case read 0.508 to 0.618: a reader looking at it sees a lower bound sitting on the line and treats the result with the caution it deserves. The interval is doing its job and reporting weak evidence as weak.

Below the threshold, the interval stops carrying that information. The six detection case read 0.611 to 0.960, which is not a marginal result; it is a confident one, and it is wrong. A reader has no signal at all that the number is untrustworthy, because the usual signal, interval width, has been destroyed by resampling six points.

So the threshold is not there to drive the error rate to zero. It is there to keep false positives in the regime where the interval still warns you about them. That is a smaller claim than the one this document originally made and it is the one the measurements support.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Widen the interval below some count. Rejected as dishonest arithmetic: it reports an interval that is not the interval the method produced, chosen to force the answer the author wanted.
  2. Raise the confidence level for sparse rules. Same objection, with extra steps, and it does not address the failure, which is that the sample may be unrepresentative rather than merely variable.
  3. Use a different interval method, such as BCa. It corrects for bias and skewness, which helps at moderate counts and does not help at six, because the problem is information rather than method.
  4. Report untunable below a minimum count. Rejected: it gives the right safety behaviour and the wrong instruction. An untunable rule needs a better signal. A rule with six detections needs a longer window. Telling an engineer the first when the second is true sends them to redesign a rule that may be perfectly good.
  5. Report a third verdict. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Three verdicts: tunable, not_tunable, and insufficient_evidence. A rule with fewer than min_true_positives_for_verdict detections is insufficient_evidence regardless of what its interval reads, and insufficient_evidence never reads as tunable.

The default is 20. It is the count above which a false tunable verdict arrives with an interval that visibly straddles chance, rather than a narrow interval around a wrong estimate. It is configuration rather than a constant, because a team with a reason can lower it and own the consequence.

It is explicitly not a count above which false positives stop. Roughly one in twenty weak rules will still read tunable, with a lower bound sitting on 0.5, and the report shows that bound so the reader can see it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The bundled corpus now reports zero untunable rules and one unmeasured one, which is a more honest description of what 12 detections in 45,000 alerts supports. The README was rewritten around that, because the previous version cited the 12 detection rule as an example of the interval working, and that example was luck rather than evidence.

The report, the chart and the CLI all carry three states. On the chart the unmeasured rule is dash dotted and amber rather than dashed and grey, and its label carries the detection count, so a reader sees immediately that the curve is built from very little.

Collapsing the three back to two would be easy and is specifically what this decision refuses. "We do not know" is an answer, and a tool that cannot say it will eventually say something worse.

Two tests pin this: one reproduces the exact six detection case and requires an unmeasured verdict, and one asserts that when a no signal rule above the threshold does read tunable, its interval lower bound sits close to 0.5 rather than comfortably above it. The second test replaced an earlier one that required no seed to come back tunable, which was asserting the overclaim this document originally made and would have failed as soon as the seed sweep widened.

The lesson, recorded because it is the more useful half: a measured zero from 60 draws is not a zero, and writing "measured" next to it does not make it one. The sweep should have been powered for the rate it was trying to rule out.

docs.title: Forensics audit: alert-triage-economics at v0.3.0
docs.text: Four personas, each auditing independently, then an integrated verdict. Graded PASS, WEAK or FAIL. Every FAIL found during this audit was fixed with its own commit before delivery, and the fix commits are named below.

docs.title: Persona 1: The Principal Engineer
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 Clone, run, verify PASS after a fix Tested literally in a clean directory from the README text alone. make verify failed with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy' while pytest run directly passed, because the console scripts pip installs bind to whichever interpreter installed them. Fixed in fix(build): run every tool through an explicit interpreter, then re-tested: 124 tests pass with no network, no credentials and no containers. 2 Architecture and design decisions PASS Three packages with a real boundary: corpus declares and generates, frontier computes, report renders. The statistics are separated from the rollup, which is why the per rule frontier is testable against worked examples independently of the stream level numbers. Five ADRs, each with rejected options. 3 Abstraction and configurability PASS Every tunable on Config from the environment with validation: minutes per alert, resample count, confidence, noise cap, minimum volume, detection minimum. The detection minimum in particular is configuration rather than a constant, so a team can lower it and own the consequence. 4 Error handling and edge cases PASS Nine documented failure modes. The interesting ones are the degenerate statistical cases: a rule with no detections, a rule below the detection minimum, a constant signal. Each has a distinct tested path and each resolves conservatively. 5 Testing PASS 124 tests, 99.3 percent branch coverage. The statistics have worked example tests small enough to check by hand, which is a convention in CONTRIBUTING rather than an accident, and it is what found the _first_loss direction bug.

docs.title: Persona 2: The UX Director and Product Thinker
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 First 30 seconds PASS Opens with the claim it refutes and the number that refutes it. The bolded one liner states the cost of halving volume, which is the whole proposition. 2 The So What of results PASS Every figure is expressed as a consequence: volume removed against detections lost, free volume converted to analyst hours at a stated rate, untunable volume as a share of the stream. The reader is never handed a statistic without its unit of decision. 3 Visual storytelling PASS The frontier chart is the repository. It draws the no information diagonal, so a rule being tuned at random is visible rather than inferred, and the three verdicts are distinguished by line style and label as well as colour. Contrast on every colour pair is measured by a tool that parses the template, and runs in CI. 4 Actionability and handoff PASS The gate verb turns the analysis into a CI check. Future Work names the first metric to watch after deploying and explains why the obvious one, volume, is the wrong choice.

docs.title: Persona 3: The Hiring Manager
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 Tutorial smell test PASS The problem is a specific sentence that appears on a great many SOC resumes, including the author's own, and the repository says so. Nothing about it is a textbook exercise. 2 Stolen Valor check PASS after a fix Was a FAIL. scipy was declared in pyproject.toml and listed in the README tech stack, and nothing imported it: the rank statistics are two lines of numpy. Removed in fix(deps): drop scipy, which was declared and never imported. This was the second repository in the batch with that exact fault, so tools/check_dependencies.py now fails CI on any declared dependency nothing uses, with an explicit list for the genuinely indirect ones so pyarrow stays distinguishable from scipy. 3 Hardest problem solved PASS Two, and the second is the better one. A one character direction error returned exactly 0.0 for every rule, a value plausible enough to be rationalised rather than noticed. Then a CI threshold check exposed the tool reporting a no signal rule as tunable on six detections with a narrow interval, which the interval mechanism could not catch by construction. Both are written up with the measurement rather than the moral. 4 One thing I will remember PASS That the repository says its own earlier correct answer was luck. The twelve detection rule was reported untunable for a reason that did not hold, and the README now tells that story rather than the flattering version it told first.

docs.title: Persona 4: The Sceptic (provenance)
docs.text:
Automated by scripts/provenance_check.py. Final run: 25 pass, 3 weak, 0 fail across 28 checks.

Two FAILs were found and fixed during this audit:

  1. scipy declared and never imported. Fixed, and generalised into a CI check so the fault cannot recur in this repository or be shipped from it.
  2. make verify failed on a fresh clone and ran a subset of CI, so a green local run did not imply a green build. Both fixed in the same commit.

The three remaining WEAKs, each with a reason:

  • 36 commits against a 40 target. The work is at real granularity and padding is detectable, so the count stands. It will exceed 40 through the issue backlog.
  • One commit subject at 73 characters. One over the limit, in a fix commit whose body carries the detail. tools/check_commit_subject.py runs as a commit-msg hook so the count cannot grow; rewriting history to shorten one subject would invalidate every clone for a character.
  • Identity placeholders unresolved. Expected: the repository was built before the GitHub account was known. tools/set_identity.sh binds every URL in one pass.

docs.title: Integrated verdict
docs.text:
Overall portfolio score: 9 out of 10.

The repository holds up to all four reads. What distinguishes it is that its two most interesting findings are both the tool failing: a statistic that was confidently wrong and a safety property that turned out to be luck. Both are written up with the measurement that exposed them, and both produced a design change rather than a patch.

It is a 9 and not a 10 for the same reason as every repository in this batch: it has not been pushed. The Actions tab is not green because no run has happened, the releases are local tags rather than GitHub Releases, and the package is publish ready rather than published.

docs.title: Critical failures (do not ship)
docs.text: None outstanding. Both FAILs found during this audit were fixed with their own commits, named above, and the affected checks re-run.

docs.title: Impact multipliers
docs.text:
1. Push and publish. Green Actions tab, three GitHub Releases from the existing annotated tags, Pages live so the badge endpoints resolve, and the package on PyPI through trusted publishing.
  2. Run against a real labelled corpus. Issue 01. Every number here is a simulation, labelled as one, and the rank invariance tests show the generator's distributional assumption is not load bearing. What a real corpus would test is whether real alert signals separate at all like these do, and the honest expectation is that they separate worse.
  3. Ship the multivariate frontier. Issue 02. One signal per rule is the simplification that made v1 shippable, and combining two conditions is what a tuning engineer actually does. It is also the point where the bootstrap cost becomes a real design problem rather than an optimisation.

docs.title: Elevator pitch
docs.text: Every SOC engineer has written "reduced alert volume by N percent" on a CV, and the sentence is almost always incomplete, because nobody collects the second half: and it cost us this many real detections. This tool computes that second half from a labelled alert history, reporting for every candidate threshold what it removes and what it costs, with an interval on everything and a CI gate so a volume target gets costed before it ships. On the bundled corpus halving alert volume costs 15.6 percent of detections, and one rule in eight turns out to have too few detections for the tool to say anything about at all, which it reports as unknown rather than guessing.
